items.title: Distinct exponential characters are linearly independent on a nonempty open set, and the real-part grouping rule
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb C^n$ ($m\ge1$) be pairwise distinct, and let $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C^q$ for some $q\ge1$ (the scalar case $q=1$ included; all statements below are componentwise). Write $\lambda_j\cdot z$ for the componentwise bilinear extension of the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the variable $z$ remains real and $e^{iw}$ for the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] at $iw$, and consider the $\mathbb C^q$-valued map $F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\,e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ on $U$. Then: (a) [Complex independence] if $F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$. (b) [Real-part grouping rule] if $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then for every $
u\in\mathbb C^n$ the grouped coefficient $$C_
u:=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u} c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{c_j}$$ vanishes; in particular $c_j=0$ whenever $\lambda_j
e-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j
otin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k
e j\}$. At a self-paired frequency $
u=-\overline
u$ the coefficient is $2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j$; in particular at $
u=0$ only the real part is constrained, and a purely imaginary coefficient is allowed. (c) [Scope] no hypothesis beyond pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and nonemptiness and openness of $U$ is used; $\lambda_j=0$ is allowed and the $\lambda_j$ need not be nonzero, ordered or normalized. The statement concerns the open set $U$ and asserts nothing on sets with empty interior, where distinct characters can agree.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct; reduce to the scalar case, conjugate the exponential by its series, prove (a) by induction on the dimension using the one-dimensional annihilating operator $\prod_{j
e j_0}(d/dt-i\lambda_j)$, then obtain (b) by applying (a) to $F+\overline F$ grouped by frequency. 1.1 Reduction to the scalar case. Both assertions are componentwise in $\mathbb C^q$: $F(z)=0$ holds if and only if every component $F_k(z)=\sum_j(c_j)_k e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ vanishes, and $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ if and only if $\operatorname{Re}F_k(z)=0$ for every $k$, while the vector $C_
u$ of clause (b) vanishes if and only if each of its components $\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}(c_j)_k+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{(c_j)_k}$ vanishes. Applying the scalar assertions $q=1$ to each component function therefore yields the general assertions, so we may and do assume $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C$ in the rest of the proof. [given, F3, algebra] 1.2 Conjugation of the exponential. For every $w\in\mathbb C$, $\overline{\exp w}=\exp\overline w$. By [F1] the complex numbers $\exp w$ and $\exp\overline w$ are the sums of the everywhere convergent series $\sum_nw^n/n!$ and $\sum_n\overline w^n/n!$, with partial sums $S_N(w)=\sum_{n\le N}w^n/n!$ and $S_N(\overline w)=\sum_{n\le N}\overline w^n/n!$; by [F2] conjugation fixes each real number $n!$ and satisfies $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$ and $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, so $\overline{S_N(w)}=S_N(\overline w)$ for every $N$. Also by [F2], $\overline u-\overline v=\overline{u-v}$ and, by the coordinate formula, $|\overline u|=\sqrt{(\operatorname{Re}u)^2+(-\operatorname{Im}u)^2}=|u|$, whence $|\overline u-\overline v|=|u-v|$. Writing $d=\overline{\exp w}-\exp\overline w$, for every $N$ we have $d=(\overline{\exp w}-S_N(\overline w))+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)=(\overline{\exp w}-\overline{S_N(w)})+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)$, so $|d|\le|\exp w-S_N(w)|+|S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w|$; given $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of convergence of the two series supplies $N$ with both summands below $\varepsilon/2$, so $|d|<\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary $|d|=0$, which forces $d=0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. [F1, F2, algebra] 1.3 Characters and the annihilating operator. For $\mu\in\mathbb C$ let $\varphi_\mu(t):=\exp(i\mu t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, the one-variable restriction of the complex exponential along the real-linear map $t\mapsto i\mu t$. By [F5], the chain rule applied to that map and the entire exponential of [F1] gives $\varphi_\mu'(t)=i\mu\exp(i\mu t)=i\mu\,\varphi_\mu(t)$, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F5] give, for any finite combination $\sum_\mu a_\mu\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients, derivative $\sum_\mu a_\mu i\mu\,\varphi_\mu$, hence $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_\mu=0$ and $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_
u=i(
u-\mu)\varphi_
u$ for all $
u\in\mathbb C$. Consequently, for pairwise distinct $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$ and a fixed $j_0$, the composed operator $L_{j_0}:=\prod_{j
e j_0}(d/dt-i\mu_j)$ is complex-linear on finite combinations and acts on $\varphi_{\mu_k}$ as multiplication by $0$ if $k
e j_0$ and by the constant $\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j)$ if $k=j_0$; that constant is nonzero because $i
e0$ and $\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j
e0$ for $j
e j_0$ by pairwise distinctness, and a product of nonzero field elements is nonzero by [F3]. [F1, F3, F5, algebra] 1.4 Induction step: reduction to a product box. Let $n\ge2$ and assume assertion (a) established in dimension $n-1$ for every number of frequencies and every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and open, fix $z^*\in U$ and, by openness, $\varepsilon>0$ with the open product box $B:=\prod_{k=1}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$; put $B':=\prod_{k=2}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $\lambda_j=(\lambda_{j1},\lambda_j')$. For each value $\mu$ in the finite set $\{\lambda_{11},\dots,\lambda_{m1}\}$ put $I_\mu:=\{j:\lambda_{j1}=\mu\}$ and $P_\mu(z'):=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$; then, by the splitting identity of [F4], the exponential addition law of [F1] and the distributivity of the finite sum, $F(z_1,z')=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu z_1}P_\mu(z')$ for every $(z_1,z')\in B$, the outer sum running over the pairwise distinct values $\mu$. [given, F1, F4, algebra] 2.1 Base case, dimension one. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, so that it contains a nonempty open interval $J$; suppose $F=\sum_{j=1}^mc_j\varphi_{\lambda_j}\equiv0$ on $U$. Fix $j_0$; then $L_{j_0}F\equiv0$ on $J$, and by step 1.3 and the linearity of $L_{j_0}$ we have $L_{j_0}F=c_{j_0} igl(\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j) igr)\varphi_{\lambda_{j_0}}$ on $J$. Choose $t_0\in J$. Evaluating there gives $c_{j_0} igl(\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j) igr)\exp(i\lambda_{j_0}t_0)=0$; cancelling the nonzero exponential by [F1] gives $c_{j_0}\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j)=0$; the second factor is a product of nonzero complex numbers, hence nonzero by [F3], so $c_{j_0}=0$ by the field property in [F3]. As $j_0$ was arbitrary, $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this proves (a) for $n=1$. [given, step 1.3, F1, F3] 2.2 The conjugate sum. Suppose now that $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ on $U$, and define $\widetilde F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}$ on $U$. For real $z$ and every $j$, step 1.2 applied to $w=i\lambda_j\cdot z$ gives $\overline{e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}}=\exp igl(\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z} igr)$, and by [F2] and the reality of $z$ we have $\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z}=\overline i\,\overline{\lambda_j\cdot z}=(-i) igl(\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z igr)=-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z$; therefore $\overline{F(z)}=\sum_j\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}=\widetilde F(z)$ on $U$ by [F2]. Since $w+\overline w=2\operatorname{Re}w$ by [F2], the hypothesis $2\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ reads $F+\widetilde F\equiv0$ on $U$. [given, step 1.2, F2] 3.1 One-dimensional slices. Suppose $F\equiv0$ on $U$, fix $z'\in B'$ and define $G(t):=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu t}P_\mu(z')$ for $t$ in the interval $J:=(z^*_1-\varepsilon,z^*_1+\varepsilon)$. By step 1.4, $G(t)=F(t,z')=0$ for every $t\in J$, and $G$ is a finite combination of the pairwise distinct characters $\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients $P_\mu(z')$; the base case of step 2.1 applied on the nonempty open interval $J$ therefore gives $P_\mu(z')=0$ for every $\mu$. As $z'\in B'$ was arbitrary, each $P_\mu$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'$. [step 2.1, step 1.4] 4.1 Induction hypothesis on each group. Fix a value $\mu$. The vectors $\lambda_j'$, $j\in I_\mu$, are pairwise distinct: if $\lambda_j'=\lambda_k'$ and $\lambda_{j1}=\lambda_{k1}=\mu$, then $\lambda_j=\lambda_k$, hence $j=k$ by pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$. The function $P_\mu=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, so assertion (a) in dimension $n-1$ gives $c_j=0$ for every $j\in I_\mu$. Every index lies in $I_{\lambda_{j1}}$, so $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this completes the induction and proves (a) in every dimension $n\ge1$. [step 3.1, step 1.4, induction] 5.1 Frequency grouping and application of part (a). Let $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be the finite set of distinct values among $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m,-\overline{\lambda_1},\dots,-\overline{\lambda_m}$, and for $
u\in\Phi$ put $C_
u:=\sum_{j:\lambda_j=
u}c_j+\sum_{j:-\overline{\lambda_j}=
u}\overline{c_j}=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{c_j}$. Regrouping the finite sum of step 2.2 over the distinct frequencies and using the bilinearity of the extended inner product in [F4] gives $F+\widetilde F=\sum_{
u\in\Phi}C_
u e^{i
u\cdot z}$ on $U$; the frequencies $
u\in\Phi$ are pairwise distinct by construction, so assertion (a) as proved in steps 2.1 and 4.1 applied to this finite combination gives $C_
u=0$ for every $
u\in\Phi$. For $
u
otin\Phi$ both defining sums are empty, so $C_
u=0$ trivially; hence $C_
u=0$ for every $
u\in\mathbb C^n$. [given, step 2.2, step 4.1, F4, algebra] 6.1 Consequences and scope. (i) If $
u=-\overline
u$ is self-paired, the condition $-\overline{\lambda_j}=
u$ is equivalent to $\lambda_j=
u$, so both sums of $C_
u$ run over the same index set and $C_
u=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}(c_j+\overline{c_j})=2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j$ by [F2]; at $
u=0$ this constrains only the real part, and the constraint is genuinely not stronger: for $m=1$, $\lambda_1=0$, $q=1$ and $c_1=i$ one has $F\equiv i$, so $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ and $C_0=c_1+\overline{c_1}=2\operatorname{Re}i=0$, a nonzero purely imaginary coefficient at frequency $0$. (ii) If $\lambda_j
e-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j
otin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k
e j\}$, then $\{k:\lambda_k=\lambda_j\}=\{j\}$ and $\{k:\lambda_k=-\overline{\lambda_j}\}=\emptyset$ (a member $k=j$ would give $\lambda_j=-\overline{\lambda_j}$, and $k
e j$ is excluded by hypothesis), so $C_{\lambda_j}=c_j+0=c_j=0$ by step 5.1, which is the stated consequence. (iii) The scope (c) holds: steps 2.1, 1.4 and 4.1 used only pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and the nonemptiness and openness of $U$, through the interval $J$ and the product box $B$; the frequencies were never assumed nonzero, ordered or normalized; the proof is a finite construction using complex arithmetic, the series for the exponential and its derivative, and no choice principle. No assertion is made for sets of empty interior: the openness of $U$ is used when a nonempty open interval and a product box are extracted from it, and the statement (c) records that distinct characters can agree on such smaller sets. [step 5.1, step 2.2, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

Read directly in the fetched PDF; for the group $(\mathbb R^n,+)$ the maps $z\mapsto e^{i\lambda\cdot z}$ are distinct characters, so the theorem is the everywhere-vanishing case of clause (a), while the item's induction supplies the localization from a nonempty open set and the real-part grouping of clause (b).

items.title: The two-equation interface admittance system: solution formulas and the normal-flux identity
items.statement:
Let $Y_1,Y_2\in\mathbb C$ with $Y_1+Y_2
e0$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t.$$ Then: (a) [Solution] If $E_i
e0$, then $$r:= rac{E_r}{E_i}= rac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t:= rac{E_t}{E_i}= rac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$ if $E_i=0$ then $E_r=E_t=0$ and the field ratios are undefined. Throughout (b)-(d), $r,t$ denote the displayed algebraic transfer coefficients $(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$, which are defined independently of $E_i$; when $E_i
e0$ they equal the field ratios of (a). (b) [Normal-flux identity] If $Y_1>0$ is real (the incident side admittance), then $$|r|^2+ rac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^2=1,$$ and explicitly $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$ and $|r|^2=1-\dfrac{4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$. The second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$; it is the normal-flux coefficient of a passive transmitted medium and may be negative for an active one, in which case $|r|>1$ and the identity carries no energy-conservation reading. (c) [Pure-imaginary admittance] If $Y_1>0$ is real and $Y_2$ is purely imaginary, then $|r|=1$, $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ and $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2}>0$; in particular $r
e0$ and $t
e0$. (d) [Real-positive specialisation] If $Y_1,Y_2>0$ are real, then $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ are real and $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$; with $Y_j=1/Z_j$, $Z_j>0$, this is $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$, $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$, $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$, in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. (e) [Scope] The lemma is pure algebra of $\mathbb C$; the labels 'incident', 'reflected' and 'transmitted' and the interpretation of the second summand as a flux fraction belong to the consuming physical theorem, not to this lemma.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct; solve the two linear equations by substitution, expand the moduli with $|z|^2=z\overline z$, and read the sign statements off the ordered-field structure of $\mathbb R$. 1.1 [Solution of the linear system] Substituting the first equation $E_r=E_t-E_i$ into the second gives $Y_1(2E_i-E_t)=Y_2E_t$, that is $2Y_1E_i=(Y_1+Y_2)E_t$ after expanding and collecting terms by the field arithmetic of [F1]. Since $Y_1+Y_2
e0$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb C$ by [F1], $E_t=2Y_1E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, and then $E_r=E_t-E_i= igl(2Y_1-(Y_1+Y_2) igr)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)=(Y_1-Y_2)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, again by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Consequences of the solution] If $E_i
e0$, dividing the two identities of step 1.1 by $E_i$ gives $r=E_r/E_i=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=E_t/E_i=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$. If $E_i=0$, the identities of step 1.1 give $E_t=0$ and $E_r=0$, so no field ratio exists; the algebraic expressions $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ remain defined because $Y_1+Y_2
e0$, and they agree with the field ratios whenever the latter exist. This proves (a) and the convention stated before (b). [step 1.1, F1, algebra] 3.1 [Modular expansions] For any $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $|z\pm w|^2=(z\pm w)(\overline z\pm\overline w)=|z|^2\pm(z\overline w+\overline z w)+|w|^2$, and $z\overline w+\overline z w=2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w)$ by [F2]; hence for real $Y_1$ and arbitrary $Y_2$, $|Y_1\pm Y_2|^2=Y_1^2\pm2Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2+|Y_2|^2$, and subtraction gives $|Y_1+Y_2|^2-|Y_1-Y_2|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2$. Moreover $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$: indeed $|zw|=|z||w|$ and $|z|^2=z\overline z$ by [F2] applied to the quotients of step 2.1 give $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ and $|t|^2=|2Y_1|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}=4Y_1^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ because $(2Y_1)\overline{(2Y_1)}=4Y_1^2$ for real $Y_1$, and the denominator is nonzero since $Y_1+Y_2
e0$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra] 4.1 [The flux identity] Assume $Y_1>0$ real. By [F2] and [F3], $|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, so $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, and the identity of step 3.1 gives $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$; adding $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ cancels the correction and yields $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$, the displayed identity and explicit formulas of (b). [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] 5.1 [Sign analysis] Still with $Y_1>0$ real: since $|t|^2>0$ by step 4.1, the second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ has the sign of $\operatorname{Re}Y_2$ by [F3], so it is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$. If $\operatorname{Re}Y_2<0$, then $|r|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>1$, and since $|r|\ge0$ and $1\ge0$, [F4] gives $|r|>1$; in that case the identity of step 4.1 has a negative transmitted term and carries no energy-conservation reading, while $|r|>1$ alone is consistent with an active transmitted model. [step 4.1, F3, F4, algebra] 5.2 [Purely imaginary admittance] Assume $Y_1>0$ real and $Y_2=i eta$ with $ eta\in\mathbb R$. Then $\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=Y_1-i eta=Y_1-Y_2$ by [F2], so $|Y_1-Y_2|=|\overline{Y_1+Y_2}|=|Y_1+Y_2|$ by [F2] and step 3.1 gives $|r|=1$; the identity of step 4.1 then gives $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ (multiplying the identity by $Y_1>0$ and using $|r|^2=1$), while $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+ eta^2)=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2)>0$ by [F2] and [F3]; hence $r
e0$ because $|r|=1$ and $t
e0$ because $|t|>0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. This proves (c); no division by $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=0$ is performed, and the case $Y_2=0$ is included with $ eta=0$. [step 4.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, algebra] 5.3 [Real-positive specialisation] Assume $Y_1,Y_2>0$ real. Then $Y_1-Y_2$ is real and $Y_1+Y_2>0$ is real and nonzero, so $r,t$ of step 2.1 are real by [F1], and step 4.1 gives $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ because $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=Y_2$. Substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ with $Z_j>0$ real, $Y_j$ is invertible and $1/Z_1\pm1/Z_2=(Z_2\pm Z_1)/(Z_1Z_2)$ by [F1], so $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ by cancellation of the nonzero factor $Z_1Z_2$; moreover $Y_2/Y_1=Z_1/Z_2$ by [F1], so the balance is $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$. These are exactly the solution formulas and the balance of [F5], so clause (d) is in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. [step 4.1, step 2.1, F1, F5, algebra] 6.1 [Scope] Clause (e) holds: the entire argument is algebra in the field $\mathbb C$ together with the ordered-field arithmetic of the real scalars $Y_1,\operatorname{Re}Y_2$; no wave model, no labelling of the amplitudes and no interpretation of the second summand is used, and no choice principle occurs, all divisions being by explicitly nonzero field elements. [given, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

items.title: Homogeneous isotropic medium parameters: phase speed, impedance, refractive index, complex propagation constant and skin depth
items.statement: Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], in its isotropic scalar case: the material is at rest in the laboratory frame, and the constitutive relations of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]] hold with constant scalars $\varepsilon>0$ (F$\,$m$^{-1}$), $\mu>0$ (H$\,$m$^{-1}$) and $\sigma\ge0$ (S$\,$m$^{-1}$), so that $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the free current is $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Write $c>0$ for the exact vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and let $\omega>0$ (s$^{-1}$) be an angular frequency. Define: (a) [Lossless parameters] with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], $$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$ $v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case. (b) [Complex propagation constant] put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and $$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$ Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$; in the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$ and $\kappa(\omega)=k(\omega)=p(\omega)$ real. (The explicit formula is the one of [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; the verification $p^{2}-q^{2}=a$, $2pq=b$ and the uniqueness of the root with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ are verified in the well-definedness paragraph below.) (c) [Skin depth] call $\delta(\omega):=1/q(\omega)$ (m) the skin depth if $\sigma>0$, and set $\delta(\omega):=+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$: for $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ and $x_3\in\mathbb R$ the modulus of $e^{i(\kappa x_3-\omega t)}$ equals $e^{-q x_3}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), so $\delta$ is the distance in which that modulus decays by the factor $1/e$ in the direction of increasing $x_3$; for $\sigma=0$ there is no attenuation and $\delta$ is infinite rather than a division by zero. (d) [Status and scope] This item fixes objects, units, branch conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity. The parameters are declared for the isotropic scalar constant-coefficient branch at rest in the laboratory frame; for $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$ the branch is, by [[post-em-material-closure]](b), a declared finite-band effective phase-response model with no universal front-speed claim, while $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ is the exact broadband case. No measured value, precision or empirical statement is included.
items.strategy: The material assumptions, the rest-frame clause, the isotropic scalar case and the finite-band caveat are those of [[post-em-material-closure]](a)-(b) read with [[def-em-polarization-magnetization|the polarization and magnetization definitions]]; the unit system and the exact constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the laboratory chart is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. The only content beyond notation is the well-definedness of $\kappa(\omega)$ in (b). With $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ one has $r+a>0$ and $(r-a)(r+a)=b^2\ge0$, so $r-a\ge0$ and both defining radicands are nonnegative. If $b>0$, the same identity gives $r-a>0$, hence $q>0$; if $b=0$, uniqueness of nonnegative roots gives $r=a$ and $q=0$. Also $p>0$ because $r+a>0$. Thus $p^{2}-q^{2}=(r+a)/2-(r-a)/2=a$ and $(2pq)^{2}=4\cdot(r+a)(r-a)/4=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$, so $2pq=b$ because $p,q\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); hence $\kappa^{2}=p^{2}-q^{2}+2ipq=a+ib$, by the field arithmetic of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. The square roots of $a+ib$ are exactly $\pm\kappa$: if $z^2=\kappa^2$, then $(z-\kappa)(z+\kappa)=0$, and the complex field property ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) gives $z=\kappa$ or $z=-\kappa$. If $k=u+iv$ with $u,v\ge0$ and $k^{2}=a+ib$, then $u^{2}-v^{2}=a$, $2uv=b$ and $u^{2}+v^{2}=|k|^{2}=|k^{2}|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=r$, where $|k^{2}|=|k|^{2}$ is the multiplicativity of the modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ is the modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; solving gives $u^{2}=(r+a)/2=p^{2}$ and $v^{2}=(r-a)/2=q^{2}$, and since $u,v,p,q\ge0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $u=p$ and $v=q$, so $k=\kappa$. In the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=0$, $p=\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}=k(\omega)$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. All divisions are by strictly positive real numbers, $v$ and $q$ are nonzero exactly where defined, and no choice principle is used.

items.physical_scope: Exact conditional statement about ideal plane-wave fields in a homogeneous isotropic Ohmic medium at rest, on the laboratory chart: the four macroscopic equations hold if and only if the four complex amplitude conditions hold, with the dispersion relation, transverse structure, lossless period-averaged energy density and flux, and the evanescent decay and normal-flux identities. Excluded: general bounded-field or finite-energy existence theory, interfaces, anisotropic or dispersive media, nonlinear response, ideal conductors, any completeness of the plane-wave family, and all empirical statements.

items.title: Phase matching at a plane interface: common tangential wavevector and frequency, the reflection law and Snell's law
items.statement:
Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the lossless isotropic scalar case: two homogeneous media at rest in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] (frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$ with constants $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$ and medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$ with constants $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$, both with $\sigma=0$, sharing the plane interface $S:=\{x_3=0\}$ with unit normal $n:=e_3$, and the plane-wave amplitude conditions and solution structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]] in each medium. Let $\omega_i,\omega_r,\omega_t>0$, $k_i,k_r,k_t\in\mathbb C^{3}$, $e_i,e_r,e_t\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$, and put $h_j:=k_j	imes e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$ for $j\in\{i,r,t\}$ where $\mu_i=\mu_r=\mu_1$ and $\mu_t=\mu_2$, so that each triple satisfies the conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c) in its own medium: $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $k_j	imes e_j=\omega_j\mu h_j$, $k_j	imes h_j=-\omega_j\varepsilon e_j$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon\mu\omega_j^{2}$ with $(\varepsilon,\mu)=(\varepsilon_1,\mu_1)$ for $j=i,r$ and $(\varepsilon_2,\mu_2)$ for $j=t$. Assume the declared normal orientation conditions $k_i\cdot n\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ and $k_r\cdot n\in\mathbb R_{<0}$; no order is placed on a complex number. Tangential components may be complex. Algebraic phase matching permits every complex transmitted wavevector satisfying its amplitude conditions and dispersion relation, including a zero normal root at critical incidence. No outgoing or non-growth condition is required here. A consuming Fresnel construction may optionally select a root $k_t\cdot n$ of $(k_t\cdot n)^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega_t^2-\kappa_t\cdot\kappa_t$, where $\kappa_t:=k_t-(k_t\cdot n)n$, with $\operatorname{Im}(k_t\cdot n)\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(k_t\cdot n)\ge0$ when its imaginary part is zero. Such a selection is a declared additional branch assumption of that construction, not a restriction on this theorem or an inferred material realization. Complex tangential phases may grow along the unbounded interface; no global tangential boundedness is asserted. Define the wave fields $E_j(x,t):=\operatorname{Re} igl(e_j e^{i(k_j\cdot x-\omega_jt)} igr)$, $H_j(x,t):=\operatorname{Re} igl(h_j e^{i(k_j\cdot x-\omega_jt)} igr)$, which are fields of [[def-em-fields]], and let $E:=E_i+E_r$, $H:=H_i+H_r$ on the medium-1 side and $E:=E_t$, $H:=H_t$ on the medium-2 side. [Interface hypothesis] assume that for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^{2}	imes I$, with $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval, the one-sided traces at $(y,0,t)$ satisfy the four stationary interface identities with no free surface charge or current, $$n\cdot igl(\varepsilon_2E_t-\varepsilon_1(E_i+E_r) igr)=0,\qquad n\cdot igl(\mu_2H_t-\mu_1(H_i+H_r) igr)=0,$$ $$n	imes igl(E_t-(E_i+E_r) igr)=0,\qquad n	imes igl(H_t-(H_i+H_r) igr)=0 .$$ Then: (a) [Phase matching] with $\kappa_j:=k_j-(k_j\cdot n)n$ the tangential wavevector, $\kappa_i=\kappa_r=\kappa_t$ and $\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t$. (b) [Geometry] if $\kappa_i
e0$ then $k_i,k_r,k_t$ all lie in the complex two-dimensional subspace $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\kappa_i,n\}$ (the real wavevectors lie in the corresponding real plane); if $\kappa_i=0$ then all three wavevectors are parallel to $n$. (c) [Propagating waves: reflection law and Snell's law] if in addition $k_i,k_r,k_t\in\mathbb R^{3}$, then with $	heta_j\in[0,\pi/2]$ defined by $\sin	heta_j=|\kappa_j|/|k_j|$ (well defined because the real dispersion relation gives $|k_j|>0$; the incident and reflected angles are below $\pi/2$, and the transmitted angle may equal $\pi/2$) one has $	heta_r=	heta_i$ and, writing $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$ and $n_j=c/v_j$ for the parameters of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], $$n_1\sin	heta_i=n_2\sin	heta_t.$$ If $	heta_i>0$, this is equivalently $\sin	heta_t/\sin	heta_i=v_2/v_1=n_1/n_2$. At normal incidence $	heta_i=0$ it gives $	heta_t=0$ without forming $0/0$. (d) [Hypotheses actually used] within the stated positive-frequency amplitude-condition setting, the only interface identities used are the two tangential identities $n	imes[E]=0$ and $n	imes[H]=0$ ; nonzero-wave hypotheses $e_j
e0$ and $k_j\cdot k_j
e0$ are retained. The two normal identities are recorded because they belong to the interface model, but they are not used. If the reflected wave is absent ($e_r=h_r=0$), the same argument matches the incident and transmitted actual waves; it does not determine the absent reflected wave's frequency or wavevector, which a Fresnel construction may conventionally assign the common phase. (e) [Scope] the wave data are given: no existence of interface-consistent data, no reflection or transmission amplitudes, no energy fluxes and no well-posedness are claimed. Complex transmitted wavevectors are covered by (a) and (b) (the evanescent case of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](e) satisfies $k_t\cdot n
e0$); the physical propagating or evanescent character of the transmitted wave, the angle selection in the real case and the amplitudes are treated by the interface items that consume this theorem. The four interface identities are the stationary plane-interface conditions of the model; for compact interfaces they follow from the distributional jump theorem [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]], and on the noncompact plane they are the stated interface hypothesis. No material dispersion, absorption, anisotropy, moving medium or nonlinearity is covered, and no empirical claim is made.
items.physical_scope: Conditional phase-matching theorem for three monochromatic plane waves at a plane interface between two homogeneous isotropic lossless media at rest, under the stated stationary interface identities: the tangential wavevector and angular frequency agree, the wavevectors are coplanar with the normal, and in the propagating case the reflection law and Snell's law follow. Excluded: reflection and transmission amplitudes, energy fluxes, existence of interface-consistent data, absorbing, dispersive, anisotropic, moving or nonlinear media, and any empirical claim.

items.title: Conducting-medium propagation: the exact attenuation constant, the skin depth and its good- and poor-conductor regimes
items.statement: Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the isotropic scalar case at rest in the laboratory frame with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma>0$, the fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and the plane-wave structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$, $n\in\mathbb R^3$ a unit vector and $k=\lambda n$, $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, and let $E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)$ be a plane-wave field satisfying the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b) with $k\cdot e=0$. Put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega>0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and let $p,q>0$ be the quantities of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Then: (a) [Exact propagation constant and decay] $\lambda^{2}=k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$, so $\lambda=\pm(p+iq)$; if $x_3':=n\cdot x$, then for $\lambda=p+iq$ $$E(x,t)=e^{-q x_3'}\,\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(p x_3'-\omega t)}\bigr),$$ so the field oscillates with wavenumber $p$ and its amplitude decays in the direction of increasing $x_3'$ at the exact rate $q$; with $\lambda=-(p+iq)$ the exact formula is $E(x,t)=e^{q x_3'}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i(-p x_3'-\omega t)})$, which grows in that direction, so the decaying branch is the one with $\lambda=p+iq$, in agreement with the selection rule of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](b). (b) [Exact skin depth] $q^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}-a\bigr)/2$, $p^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)/2$, $pq=b/2=\mu\sigma\omega/2$, and the skin depth of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] equals the exact closed expression $$\delta(\omega)=\frac{1}{q}=\frac{\sqrt{2\,(r+a)}}{b}=\frac{\sqrt{2\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)}}{\mu\sigma\omega}.$$ (c) [Good-conductor regime] put $t:=a/b=\varepsilon\omega/\sigma>0$. For every $t\le1/4$ the exact value satisfies the explicit bounds $$\bigl|q-\sqrt{b/2}\bigr|\le2t\sqrt{b/2}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}},\qquad \bigl|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}\bigr|\le4t\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}} ;$$ equivalently $\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)}\,\bigl(1+O(\varepsilon\omega/\sigma)\bigr)$ in the declared regime $\varepsilon\omega/\sigma\le1/4$, with the displayed explicit remainder bounds. (d) [Poor-conductor regime] put $t':=b/a=\sigma/(\varepsilon\omega)>0$. For every $t'\le1/2$ the exact value satisfies $$\Bigl|q-\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}\Bigr|\le\frac{t'^{2}}{4}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}},\qquad\Bigl|\delta-\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}\Bigr|\le\frac{t'^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}},$$ so in this regime $\delta$ is frequency-independent up to the displayed relative error $O\bigl((\sigma/(\varepsilon\omega))^{2}\bigr)$. (e) [Phase relation for a real amplitude] if $e\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\lambda=p+iq$, then $$E(x,t)=e^{-q x_3'}e\cos(px_3'-\omega t),\qquad H(x,t)=\frac{e^{-q x_3'}}{\mu\omega}\bigl(p\cos(px_3'-\omega t)-q\sin(px_3'-\omega t)\bigr)\,(n\times e),$$ and the ratio of the quadrature to the in-phase coefficient is $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$ with $1-2t\le q/p\le1$ for every $t\le1/2$; in particular $q/p\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$, so the magnetic scalar factor is $\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\cos(px_3'-\omega t+\eta)$ with $\eta:=\arctan(q/p)\to\pi/4$ (45 degrees), not a 90-degree quadrature phase shift. At fixed position with the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention this corresponds to the stated signed $+\eta$ phase in the decreasing phase variable. (f) [Limits and scope] for $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$, and the approximations of (c) and (d) are not applicable; the ideal-conductor limit $\sigma\to\infty$ is not covered by this theorem, which works inside the finite-Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] (a separate boundary model is needed for an ideal conductor); the frequency dependence of $\sigma$ (Drude or other) is not supplied, and $\sigma$ is the declared constant of the branch; the conclusions are exact identities for the ideal plane-wave field and carry no empirical content, no measured conductivity and no claim about any laboratory field.
items.strategy: Proof technique: direct; substitute the concrete data into the medium plane-wave theorem, extract the decaying root via Euler's Cartesian form, and bound the exact radicals with elementary square-root inequalities. 1.1 [Propagation constant and decay, part (a)] By [F1], $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$, and since $k=\lambda n$ with $n\cdot n=1$ the bilinear expansion gives $\lambda^{2}=k\cdot k=a+ib$; by [F1] and [F5] with [F3], the solutions of $z^{2}=a+ib$ are exactly $z=\pm(p+iq)$. Writing $x_3'=n\cdot x$, so that $k\cdot x=\lambda x_3'$, the exponent is $i(k\cdot x-\omega t)=i\lambda x_3'-i\omega t$; for $\lambda=p+iq$ this is $-qx_3'+i(px_3'-\omega t)$, and the Cartesian form [F2] gives $e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}=e^{-qx_3'}(\cos(px_3'-\omega t)+i\sin(px_3'-\omega t))$, whence $E=e^{-qx_3'}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(px_3'-\omega t)}\bigr)$ componentwise; the amplitude factor $e^{-qx_3'}$ decreases as $x_3'$ increases because $q>0$ by [F1]. For $\lambda=-(p+iq)$ the same computation gives $i\lambda x_3'-i\omega t=qx_3'+i(-px_3'-\omega t)$ and $E=e^{qx_3'}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i(-px_3'-\omega t)})$, which grows in the direction of increasing $x_3'$; the decaying branch is therefore $\lambda=p+iq$, matching the root selection of [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra] 2.1 [Exact skin depth, part (b)] By [F1], $q^{2}=(r-a)/2$ and $p^{2}=(r+a)/2$ with $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$; multiplying, $(pq)^{2}=\bigl(r^{2}-a^{2}\bigr)/4=b^{2}/4$, and since $p,q\ge0$ and $b>0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root in [F4] gives $pq=b/2=\mu\sigma\omega/2$. For the skin depth $\delta=1/q$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](c): $\delta^{2}=1/q^{2}=2/(r-a)=2(r+a)/\bigl((r-a)(r+a)\bigr)=2(r+a)/b^{2}$, where $(r-a)(r+a)=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$ by [F4]; since $\delta>0$ and $b>0$, taking the nonnegative square root gives $\delta=\sqrt{2(r+a)}/b$, and substituting $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}$ and $b=\mu\sigma\omega$ gives the displayed closed form. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra] 3.1 [Ratio identities] With $t=a/b>0$ one has $r=b\sqrt{1+t^{2}}$ because $r^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=b^{2}(t^{2}+1)$ and both sides are nonnegative, by [F4]; hence $q^{2}=(r-a)/2=\tfrac{b}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)$ and $\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t=\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}+t\bigr)^{-1}$, the second identity because $\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}+t\bigr)=1+t^{2}-t^{2}=1$ with all factors positive by [F4] and [F1]. Moreover $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$: indeed $q^{2}/p^{2}=(r-a)/(r+a)$, and the same rationalisation gives $(r-a)/(r+a)=\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)^{2}$, so the positive quantities $q/p$ and $\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$ have equal squares and are equal by [F4]. With $s=t'=b/a>0$ one has analogously $r=a\sqrt{1+s^{2}}$ and $q^{2}=\tfrac{a}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1\bigr)$. Writing $q_{t}:=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$, the identity $q_{t}=\frac{\sqrt{a}\,s}{2}$ holds: expanding $\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}$ and $s=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon\omega}$ by [F1] gives $\frac{\sqrt a\,s}{2}=\frac{\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\sigma}{2\varepsilon\omega}=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$; hence $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}=\frac{2(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1)}{s^{2}}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+s^{2}}}$ by the same rationalisation. [step 2.1, F1, F4, algebra] 4.1 [Good-conductor bounds, part (c)] For $t\ge0$ one has $1\le\sqrt{1+t^{2}}\le1+t$: the left inequality because $1\le1+t^{2}$ and both sides are nonnegative, the right because $1+t^{2}\le(1+t)^{2}=1+2t+t^{2}$, both by [F4]. Hence $\frac{1}{1+2t}\le\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\le\frac{1}{1+t}\le1$ by step 3.1 and [F4], and $\frac{1}{1+2t}\ge1-2t$ because $0\le1-2t\le1$ and $(1-2t)(1+2t)=1-4t^{2}\le1$ for $t\le1/2$; therefore $\sqrt{1-2t}\le\frac{q}{\sqrt{b/2}}\le1$, that is $\sqrt{b/2}\sqrt{1-2t}\le q\le\sqrt{b/2}$. For $t\le1/4$ one has $1-2t\ge0$ and $(1-2t)^{2}\le1-2t$, so $\sqrt{1-2t}\ge1-2t$ by [F4], giving $\bigl|q-\sqrt{b/2}\bigr|\le2t\sqrt{b/2}$ with the stated equivalent form since $\sqrt{b/2}=\sqrt{\mu\sigma\omega/2}$. For $\delta=1/q$ one has $\sqrt{2/b}\le\delta\le\frac{\sqrt{2/b}}{1-2t}$ from the bound on $q$ and [F4]; and $\frac{1}{1-2t}\le1+4t$ for $t\le1/4$ because $1\le(1+4t)(1-2t)=1+2t-8t^{2}$, i.e. $0\le2t(1-4t)$, by [F4]; hence $\bigl|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}\bigr|\le4t\sqrt{2/b}$ with the stated equivalent form. [step 3.1, F1, F4, algebra] 4.2 [Poor-conductor bounds, part (d)] By step 3.1, $q^{2}=\tfrac{a}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1\bigr)$ and $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+s^{2}}}$ with $q_{t}=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$, $s=t'=b/a>0$. Since $\sqrt{1+s^{2}}\ge1$, the ratio is at most $1$, so $q\le q_{t}$; and $\sqrt{1+s^{2}}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ because $1+s^{2}\le\bigl(1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}\bigr)^{2}=1+s^{2}+\frac{s^{4}}{4}$, so $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}\ge\frac{2}{2+\frac{s^{2}}{2}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}}$; for $s^{2}\le1$ (which holds when $s\le1/2$) one has $\frac{1}{1+s^{2}/4}\ge1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}$ since $\bigl(1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}\bigr)\bigl(1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}\bigr)=1-\frac{s^{4}}{16}\le1$ with $1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}\ge0$; therefore $q/q_{t}\ge1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}$, i.e. $\bigl|q-q_{t}\bigr|\le\frac{s^{2}}{4}q_{t}$. For $\delta=1/q$ and $\delta_{t}=1/q_{t}$ we get $\delta/\delta_{t}=q_{t}/q\le\frac{1}{1-s^{2}/4}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ whenever $s^{2}\le1$ (since $\frac{1}{1-s^{2}/4}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ is equivalent to $1\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}-\frac{s^{4}}{8}$, true for $s^{2}\le2$), whence $\bigl|\delta-\delta_{t}\bigr|\le\frac{s^{2}}{2}\delta_{t}$; substituting $\delta_{t}=\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}$ gives both displayed bounds, by [F4] throughout. [step 3.1, F4, algebra] 5.1 [Phase relation, part (e)] Assume $e\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\lambda=p+iq$; by [F1], $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)=\lambda\,(n\times e)/(\omega\mu)$ because $k=\lambda n$ and $n\times e$ is real, and the exponent is computed as in step 1.1. Writing $\theta:=px_3'-\omega t$ and using $\lambda/(\mu\omega)=(p+iq)/(\mu\omega)$ with real $p,q$, the Cartesian form [F2] gives $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((p+iq)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)=p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta$, so $E=e^{-qx_3'}e\cos\theta$ and $H=e^{-qx_3'}(p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta)(n\times e)/(\mu\omega)$, the two displayed identities. By step 3.1, $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$, and the bounds $1-2t\le q/p\le1$ for $t\le1/2$ are the ones established in step 4.1 for the same quantity; as $t\downarrow0$ the inequality $0\le\sqrt{1+t^2}-1=t^2/(\sqrt{1+t^2}+1)\le t^2/2$ gives $|\sqrt{1+t^2}-t-1|\le t+t^2/2\to0$, so $\eta:=\arctan(q/p)$ tends to $\arctan 1=\pi/4$ by the continuity of $\arctan$ in [F6]. Put $r:=q/p>0$ and $\eta=\arctan r\in(0,\pi/2)$; by [F6], $\sin\eta=r\cos\eta$, and the Pythagorean identity $\sin^{2}\eta+\cos^{2}\eta=1$ with $\cos\eta>0$ gives $\cos\eta=1/\sqrt{1+r^{2}}$ and $\sin\eta=r/\sqrt{1+r^{2}}$; equivalently $\cos\eta=p/\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$ and $\sin\eta=q/\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$, since $\sqrt{1+r^{2}}=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}/p$ with $p>0$ by [F4]. The addition formula of [F6] then gives $\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}\cos(\theta+\eta)=p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta$, which is the stated form of the magnetic scalar factor. [given, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F4, F6, F7, algebra] 6.1 [Limits and scope, part (f)] Clause (f): for $\sigma=0$ the definition of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] gives $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$, and the divisions and bounds of steps 3.1-4.2 use $b>0$, $q>0$ and are not evaluated at zero; the limit $\sigma\to\infty$ is outside the finite-Ohmic branch and the frequency dependence of $\sigma$ is not supplied; all identities are exact for the plane-wave field and involve no measurement, material data or empirical statement, and no choice principle is used since every quantity is defined by explicit formulas in the given scalars. [given, step 4.2, F1, F8] ∎
items.physical_scope: Exact conditional statement about a monochromatic plane-wave field in a homogeneous isotropic Ohmic medium at rest with constant scalar eps,mu>0 and sigma>0: the exact complex propagation constant and decay, the closed-form skin depth, explicit bounded remainder inequalities in the good-conductor regime eps*omega/sigma<=1/4 and the poor-conductor regime sigma/(eps*omega)<=1/2, and the phase relation. Excluded: sigma=0 (no attenuation, infinite skin depth), the ideal-conductor limit, frequency-dependent or tensor conductivity, anisotropy, dispersion, nonlinearity, any laboratory material and all empirical claims.

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos lecture notes (2026 author-hosted revision, 236 pp.)
references.locator: §7.6.2 printed pp. 207-209: the conductor ansatz with $J=\sigma(\omega)E$, the effective permittivity $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}=\varepsilon+i\sigma/\omega$, the dispersion relation (7.54), the low-frequency Drude regime $\sigma(\omega)\approx\sigma_{\mathrm{DC}}$ with $k=k_1+ik_2=\sqrt{\mu\omega\sigma_{\mathrm{DC}}/2}\,(1+i)$, the skin depth $\delta=1/k_2=\sqrt{2/(\mu\omega\sigma_{\mathrm{DC}})}$ and the $\pi/4$ phase statement; the high-frequency plasma-frequency discussion is disposed separately in the coverage file and is not used here.

references.title: David J. Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 3rd edition (Prentice Hall, 1999, 596-page retained scan)
references.locator: §9.4.1 printed pp. 393-396: the modified wave equations (9.122), the attenuated plane waves (9.123), the complex wave number (9.124) $k^{2}=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$, the decomposition $k=k+i\kappa$ (9.125) and the skin depth $d=1/\kappa$ (9.128); Problems 9.19(a),(b),(c) printed pp. 395-396 state the poor-conductor frequency-independent skin depth, the good-conductor depth $\lambda/2\pi$ and the $\pi/4$ phase lag. Retained scan with OCR noise; the exact formulas were cross-checked against Tong and against the local computations in the batch notes.

items.title: Normal-incidence amplitudes and the flux budget, with the Ohmic transmitting medium
items.statement: Assume the following plane-interface material setting, with the same explicitly adopted stationary interface identities as [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] (including its absent-wave qualification), at normal incidence: medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$ with $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$, $\sigma_1=0$, medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$ with $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$ and either $\sigma_2=0$ (lossless) or $\sigma_2>0$ (Ohmic), both homogeneous and at rest in the laboratory chart, with the plane interface $S=\{x_3=0\}$ and normal $n=e_3$. Let $\omega_i,\omega_r,\omega_t>0$ and let three plane waves of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]] be given with wavevectors $k_i=k_1n$ ($k_1>0$), $k_r=-k_1n$ and $k_t=k\,n$, where for $\sigma_2=0$ one takes $k=\omega_t/v_2>0$ and for $\sigma_2>0$ one takes $k=\kappa_2(\omega_t)=p+iq$ with the complex propagation constant of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]; amplitudes $e_i\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ and $e_r,e_t\in\mathbb C^{3}$ and $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$ satisfying the conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c) in their media, and the four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] holding on $\mathbb R^{2}\times I$ for a nonempty open interval $I$. Then: (a) [Common frequency] The transmitted amplitude is nonzero and $\omega_i=\omega_t=:\omega$ for some $\omega>0$. If $e_r\ne0$, then $\omega_r=\omega$ as well; if $e_r=0$, assign $\omega_r=\omega$ conventionally, since an absent field cannot determine a frequency. Matching is proved directly from the interface characters, so the lossless-only physical scope of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] is not used to infer the Ohmic branch. (b) [Amplitude system and solution] all three electric amplitudes are tangential to $S$, and the two tangential interface identities reduce to $$e_i+e_r=e_t,\qquad Y_1\,(e_i-e_r)=Y_2\,e_t,\qquad Y_1:=\frac{k_1}{\mu_1\omega}>0,\qquad Y_2:=\frac{k}{\mu_2\omega};$$ hence $e_r=r\,e_i$ and $e_t=t\,e_i$ with the complex scalars $$r=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$ in particular the reflected and transmitted electric phasors are parallel to the incident one (normal-incidence polarisation preservation), and $t\ne0$. The reflection coefficient is zero exactly when $Y_1=Y_2$, in particular at a lossless impedance-matched interface; the zero reflected field remains part of the theorem. (c) [Lossless transmitting medium] if $\sigma_2=0$ then $Y_2=1/Z_2>0$ with $Z_2=\sqrt{\mu_2/\varepsilon_2}$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], so $$r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}\in\mathbb R,\qquad t=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}\in\mathbb R,$$ in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]; the period-$T$ averaged normal fluxes of the stored-energy model, $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d), [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]), are $\langle S_i\cdot n\rangle=\frac{|e_i|^{2}}{2Z_1}$, $\langle S_r\cdot n\rangle=-\frac{|e_r|^{2}}{2Z_1}$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=\frac{|e_t|^{2}}{2Z_2}$, and with $R:=r^{2}$, $T:=\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}t^{2}=\frac{4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^{2}}$ one has $R+T=1$; $R$ is the reflected and $T$ the transmitted fraction of the incident normal averaged flux. (d) [Ohmic transmitting medium] if $\sigma_2>0$ then $Y_2=\kappa_2(\omega)/(\mu_2\omega)$ has $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)>0$, and $$r=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad |r|^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^{2}=1 .$$ The second summand is the fraction of the incident period-averaged normal flux that enters the conductor at the interface; the transmitted field has the exact decay factor $e^{-qx_3}$ (the explicit factorization $e^{i(p+iq)x_3}=e^{-qx_3}e^{ipx_3}$) and, by the Ohmic dissipation clause of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]], the entering flux is absorbed in the conductor: the reflected fraction $|r|^{2}$ and the absorbed fraction $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^{2}$ add to $1$. (e) [Scope] no existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data, no oblique incidence, no anisotropic or dispersive media, no ideal conductor ($\sigma_2=\infty$), no nonlinear response and no empirical claim is made. The interface identities are the stationary plane-interface conditions of the model, supplied for compact interfaces by [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]; the flux identities are the model's stored-energy and Ohmic-dissipation reading, not an observational claim.

items.physical_scope: Conditional normal-incidence reflection and transmission theorem at a plane interface between two homogeneous isotropic scalar media at rest, the second either lossless or Ohmic: the amplitude system, the reflection and transmission amplitudes, the flux budget R+T=1 in the lossless case and |r|^2+(ReY_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1 with the absorbed fraction in the Ohmic case. Excluded: oblique incidence, anisotropic, dispersive or nonlinear media, ideal conductors, mobile media, existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data, and all empirical claims.

Let $\omega>0$, let $\kappa\in\mathbb R^{2}$ (identified with the tangential plane $\{x_3=0\}$) satisfy $0<|\kappa|<K_1:=\omega(\varepsilon_1\mu_1)^{1/2}$, put $k_{13}:=\sqrt{K_1^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0$ and define wavevectors $$k_i:=\kappa+k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_r:=\kappa-k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_t:=\kappa+k_{t3}\,n,$$ where $k_{t3}\in\mathbb C$ satisfies $k_{t3}^{2}=K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}$ with $K_2:=\omega(\varepsilon_2\mu_2)^{1/2}$ and is selected by non-growth in the $x_3>0$ half-space: $$k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|<K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=0\ \ (|\kappa|=K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=i eta,\  eta:=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|>K_2).$$ [This transmitted phase data is the interface-consistent, bounded choice: the propagating and evanescent branches of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d),(e); the common $(\kappa,\omega)$ is declared here for each actual wave, also when a reflected amplitude is zero or the critical transmitted root is zero; the nonzero phase-matching theorem explains this matching where its hypotheses apply, and an absent reflected field has no determined phase labels.] Fix the orthonormal tangential frame $\hat\kappa:=\kappa/|\kappa|$ and $\hat y:=n	imes\hat\kappa$, and consider the two polarisations: (s) [transverse electric] $e_i=E_i\hat y$, $e_r=E_r\hat y$, $e_t=E_t\hat y$ with $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$, $E_i

Proof technique: direct; verify the amplitude conditions for the two polarisation families, reduce the tangential interface identities to scalar admittance systems in the fixed frame, and read off the propagating, Brewster, evanescent and critical cases from the admittance algebra and the medium plane-wave structure. 1.1 [Both polarisation families satisfy the amplitude conditions] For (s), $k_j\cdot e_j=E_j\,k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ because $k_j=\kappa+k_{j3}n$ and $\hat y\perp\kappa,n$; and $k_j	imes e_j=E_jk_j	imes\hat y=E_j(\kappa	imes\hat y+k_{j3}n	imes\hat y)=E_j(|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x)$ by [F5], which equals $\omega\mu_jh_j$ with $h_j=k_j	imes e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$ by definition. items.title: Numerical check of the good-conductor skin-depth bounds and the $\sigma=0$ exclusion
items.statement: Adopt the isotropic scalar Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] at rest and the exact quantities of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]]. Let the declared parameters be $$\varepsilon=4\ \mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \mu=1\ \mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \sigma=100\ \mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \omega=3\ \mathrm s^{-1};$$ these are declared model parameters of the illustration, not measured values of any material. The numerical evaluations below use these SI units: $a,b,r$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $p,q$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and $\delta$ has unit m; $t=a/b$ is dimensionless. Then: (i) $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}=36$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega=300$, $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=3/25=0.12\le1/4$, so the good-conductor regime of [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](c) applies; (ii) the exact propagation and attenuation constants are $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$ and $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, with $pq=b/2=150$ exactly; the decimal evaluations $r\approx302.15228$, $p\approx13.00293$, $q\approx11.53586$ satisfy $q<\sqrt{b/2}=\sqrt{150}\approx12.24745$ with $$|q-\sqrt{150}|\approx0.71159\le 2t\sqrt{150}=0.24\sqrt{150}\approx2.93939,$$ and for the skin depth $\delta=1/q\approx0.08669$ against $\sqrt{2/b}=1/\sqrt{150}\approx0.08165$ one has $$|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\approx0.00504\le 4t\sqrt{2/b}=0.48\sqrt{2/b}\approx0.03919 .$$ Thus the exact skin depth satisfies the stated good-conductor bound with the margin predicted by the theorem. (iii) for $\sigma=0$ (same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$) one has $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](c); the inequalities of (ii) do not apply, consistently with the exclusion recorded in [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](f). (iv) [Scope] the computation is an exact check of the stated inequalities for the declared model parameters (with dimensionless ratio $t$); it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical claim, and the decimal evaluations are displayed only as approximate illustrations of the exact expressions.
items.strategy: Proof technique: direct substitution in the exact identities and bounds of the skin-depth theorem, with the decimal displays read as roundings of the exact radicals. Given: The declared parameters $\varepsilon=4$, $\mu=1$, $\sigma=100$, $\omega=3$ as the stated dimensionless representatives of the SI quantities of the Example, the branch assumption of [[post-em-material-closure]], and the exact quantities $a,b,r,p,q,\delta,t$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]]. [A1] The declared Ohmic branch with $\sigma>0$: the plane-wave attenuation theorem [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]] holds, with its clauses (a)-(f) as stated, in particular the exact identities of (b) and the good-conductor bounds of (c) for $t\le1/4$. [F1] The medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega$, $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$ for $\sigma>0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ for $\sigma=0$; $t:=a/b$. 1.1 [Substitution, clause (i)] By [F1], $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2=1\cdot4\cdot9=36$ and $b=\mu\sigma\omega=1\cdot100\cdot3=300$; hence $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{36^2+300^2}=\sqrt{1296+90000}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=36/300=3/25$. The regime condition $3/25\le1/4$ is $12\le25$ after multiplying by $100$, so the good-conductor bounds of [A1](c) apply. [given, A1, F1, algebra] 1.2 [Exact identities, clause (ii)] By [F1] and [A1](b), $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}-36)/2}$ and $pq=b/2=150$ exactly. Since $91296<336^2=112896$, positivity and the square-root order give $r=\sqrt{91296}<336$, hence $q^2=(r-36)/2<300/2=b/2$, so $q<\sqrt{150}=\sqrt{b/2}$; and the exact bounds of [A1](c) read $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}}$. [A1, F1, algebra] 1.3 [The $\sigma=0$ exclusion, clause (iii)] For the same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$ and $\sigma=0$, [F1] gives $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [F1]; the identities and bounds of [A1](b),(c) carry the hypothesis $b>0$, equivalently $\sigma>0$, and are not evaluated at $b=0$, which is the exclusion recorded in [A1](f). [given, A1, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Decimal displays and the bound comparisons] The decimal numbers displayed in clause (ii) of the Example are the stated roundings of the exact quantities $r=\sqrt{91296}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$, $\sqrt{150}$ and $\sqrt{2/300}$; reading them as roundings, the comparisons $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}$ displayed there are instances of the exact inequalities of step 1.2, and the numerical magnitudes quoted in the Example are not independent assertions of exact decimal arithmetic. In particular the inequalities hold with the margin predicted by [A1](c) for the declared dimensionless ratio $t=3/25$. [step 1.2, A1, algebra] 3.1 [Scope, clause (iv)] The computation used only the declared parameters, the branch assumption [A1] and the exact definitions [F1]; it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical or statistical claim, and the decimal displays of the Example are approximate illustrations of the exact expressions, as stated. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 1.3, A1, F1] ∎

items.title: The Brewster angle at an equal-permeability interface and the surviving $s$-reflection
items.statement: Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with two lossless media at rest, equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared refractive indices $n_1=1$, $n_2=3/2$ (declared model parameters, not optical measurements), so that $\varepsilon_j=n_j^{2}/(c^{2}\mu)$ and $K_j=n_j\omega/c$ in the notation of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Then: (i) [Brewster angle] by [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]](c) the TM amplitude vanishes exactly at the unique angle $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ with $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1=3/2$, i.e. $\sin\theta_B=3/\sqrt{13}$, $\cos\theta_B=2/\sqrt{13}$; the transmitted angle satisfies $n_1\sin\theta_B=n_2\sin\theta_t$, hence $\sin\theta_t=2/\sqrt{13}$, and $\theta_B+\theta_t=\pi/2$; (ii) [Amplitudes] at $\theta_i=\theta_B$ one has $Y^{p}_1=Y^{p}_2=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$, hence $r_p=0$ and $t_p=1$; the remaining $s$-amplitudes are $Y^{s}_1=2/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^{s}_2=9/(2\sqrt{13}c\mu)$ and $$r_s=\frac{2/\sqrt{13}-9/(2\sqrt{13})}{2/\sqrt{13}+9/(2\sqrt{13})}=-\frac{5}{13},\qquad t_s=\frac{8}{13};$$ (iii) [Flux budget] with $R_s=|r_s|^{2}=25/169$ and $T_s=(Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=(9/4)(64/169)=144/169$ one has $R_s+T_s=169/169=1$ exactly, while the TM channel has $R_p=0$, $T_p=1$; (iv) [Scope] the numbers are declared model parameters; the example is a deterministic computation of the classical interface model, reports no measurement, and a pure TM incident wave has zero reflected field at the Brewster angle. For incident data with a nonzero TE component, the surviving reflected field is TE-polarised because $r_p=0$ and $r_s\ne0$; no unpolarised-beam statistics are modelled here.

items.title: Total internal reflection: decaying transmitted field, vanishing normal flux and the reflection phase
items.statement: Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared indices $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$ (declared model parameters, not measurements), choose the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, so $\hat\kappa=e_1$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_2$, and take the transverse-electric polarisation $e_j=E_j\hat y$. Let the incidence angle be given by $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, which exceeds the critical angle $\theta_c$ with $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3$, so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i=(6/5)(\omega/c)>(\omega/c)=K_2$. Then with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=(\omega/c)(3/2)(3/5)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$: (i) [Reflection] $Y^{s}_1=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^{s}_2=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $$r_s=\frac{9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |r_s|=1,\qquad t_s=\frac{9/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |t_s|^{2}=\frac{324}{125};$$ the reflection factor is the phase $r_s=e^{-2i\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\arctan\!\bigl(2\sqrt{11}/9\bigr)\approx0.63514703$ (about $36.39124^\circ$), i.e. the reflected wave acquires the phase $-2\varphi\approx-1.27029406$ (about $-72.78249^\circ$); (ii) [Transmitted field] the transmitted field is $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with $\beta=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$: it decays by the factor $e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}\approx0.51514$ when $x_3$ increases by $c/\omega$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, while its tangential averaged flux is positive, $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}\,\frac{(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}=e^{-2\beta x_3}\frac{3|E_t|^{2}}{5\mu c}$; (iii) [Flux budget] $|r_s|^{2}+(\operatorname{Re}Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=1+0=1$, so the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the evanescent field carries a tangential averaged flux only; (iv) [Scope] the example is an exact deterministic computation of the lossless interface model for declared parameters; it reports no measurement, and the presence of a tangential evanescent flux is not a claim about information speed or signal propagation.
items.strategy: Proof technique: direct substitution in the oblique-incidence and medium plane-wave theorems with exact rational and quadratic-irrational arithmetic, and an explicit phase computation via Euler's form. Given: The lossless two-media setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu>0$, $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$, the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, the transverse-electric data $e_j=E_j\hat y$ with $\hat y=e_2$, and the incidence data $\sin\theta_i=4/5$. [A1] The oblique-incidence theorem [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]]: clause (a) and (d) give $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, the amplitude formulas, and in the evanescent branch $|r_s|=1$, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)>0$ together with the flux budget; clause (d) also records that the transmitted field decays and its normal averaged flux vanishes. [A2] The medium plane-wave structure [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: the transmitted evanescent field of clause (e) with the substitution $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$: the exact factorization, the vanishing normal component $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle\equiv0$ and the positive tangential averaged flux $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=|\kappa_0||e|^2e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}/(2\mu\omega)$ for the transverse-electric data $e=E_0(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$. [F1] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega n_j/c$, $k_{13}^2=K_1^2-|\kappa|^2$, $\beta^2=|\kappa|^2-K_2^2$, $k_{t3}=i\beta$ and $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$. [F2] Complex arithmetic and modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]): $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z|^2=z\overline z$ and $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ only for $z=0$; in particular a complex number of modulus one is nonzero and the sum of a complex number and its conjugate is twice its real part. [F3] Trigonometry and phases: $\arctan$ is the principal inverse tangent with $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]); and for real $y$, $\exp(iy)=\cos y+i\sin y$ with $|\exp(iy)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). 1.1 [The geometry and the evanescent data] With $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$ one has $\hat\kappa=e_1$, $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_3\times e_1=e_2$; $K_1=(3/2)(\omega/c)$, $K_2=\omega/c$ by [F1], so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i$ with $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, and $|\kappa|>K_2$ because $6/5>1$. Hence the evanescent branch applies: $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}=\sqrt{(36/25-1)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{11/25}\,(\omega/c)=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=\sqrt{K_1^2-|\kappa|^2}=\sqrt{(9/4-36/25)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{81/100}\,(\omega/c)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$; the critical angle satisfies $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3<4/5=\sin\theta_i$, both angles being in $(0,\pi/2)$. [given, A1, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Admittances and reflection data, clause (i)] By [A1](a) and [F1], $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu\omega)=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $t_s=2Y^s_1/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=(9/(5\mu c))/((9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)/(\mu c))=(9/5)/(9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)$; the numerator $9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5$ of $r_s=(Y^s_1-Y^s_2)/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)$ is the complex conjugate of its denominator, so $|r_s|=1$ by [F2] (and [A1](d)). For the transmitted modulus, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)$ by [A1](d); computing $(Y^s_1)^2=81/(100\mu^2c^2)$ and $|Y^s_2|^2=11/(25\mu^2c^2)=44/(100\mu^2c^2)$ gives $|t_s|^2=(324/100)/(125/100)=324/125$. [step 1.1, A1, F2, algebra] 2.2 [The transmitted field and its fluxes, clause (ii)] By $|t_s|^2$-normalised data we take the transmitted electric amplitude $E_t\hat y$ with $E_t=t_sE_i$; the evanescent structure of [A2] applied with $n'=n=e_3$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$, $\beta$ as in step 1.1 and $e=E_t\hat y=E_t(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$ gives exactly $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$, the identity $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, and the tangential averaged flux $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}|\kappa||E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)$; substituting $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ gives $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)=e^{-2\beta x_3}3|E_t|^2/(5\mu c)$. The decay over a distance $c/\omega$ is the factor $e^{-\beta c/\omega}=e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}$, whose decimal display in clause (ii) is the stated rounding. [step 1.1, A1, A2, algebra] 3.1 [The reflection phase, clause (i)] Put $Y_1:=9/10$ and $\beta':=\sqrt{11}/5$ in the units $1/(\mu c)$ and $\alpha:=\beta'/Y_1=2\sqrt{11}/9$, so that $r_s=(1-i\alpha)/(1+i\alpha)$; let $\varphi:=\arctan\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $w:=1+i\alpha$, $|w|=\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}$. By [F3], $\tan\varphi=\alpha$ and $1+\tan^2\varphi=\sec^2\varphi$, so $\cos^2\varphi=1/(1+\alpha^2)=1/|w|^2$; since $\cos\varphi>0$ (cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ and $\varphi\in(0,\pi/2)$), $\cos\varphi=1/|w|$ and $\sin\varphi=\alpha\cos\varphi=\alpha/|w|$. Euler's form of [F3] then gives $w=|w|(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)=|w|e^{i\varphi}$ and $\overline w=|w|e^{-i\varphi}$ by [F2], so $r_s=\overline w/w=e^{-2i\varphi}$. The decimal values displayed in clause (i) are the stated roundings of $\varphi=\arctan(2\sqrt{11}/9)$ and of the reflected phase $-2\varphi$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra] 4.1 [Flux budget and scope, clauses (iii)-(iv)] By [A1](d), $|r_s|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2/Y^s_1)|t_s|^2=1$; here $\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2=0$ by step 2.1, so the identity reads $1+0=1$: the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the tangential averaged flux of step 2.2 is positive and transports no normal flux. All quantities are declared model parameters; the computation is deterministic classical interface algebra, reports no measurement, and neither the tangential evanescent flux nor the reflection phase is a claim about information speed, signal propagation or empirical data. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, F2] ∎
items.physical_scope: Deterministic example of total internal reflection in the lossless interface model for declared indices n_1=3/2, n_2=1 at sin(theta_i)=4/5: the unit-modulus reflection factor with its phase, the evanescent transmitted field with decay factor e^{-beta x_3}, the vanishing normal and positive tangential averaged fluxes. Excluded: measured indices, absorption, information-speed or signal-propagation claims, and every empirical statement.
